questions.text: A teacher keeps the marks of 80 students in cells B2:B81 of an Excel sheet and wants to know how many students scored more than 60. Which formula should be used?
questions.explanation: COUNTIF(range, criteria) counts the cells that meet one condition. SUMIF would return the total of the qualifying marks.
steps: Spot what the question tests: COUNT, COUNTA, COUNTIF, SUMIF.
Option B (=COUNT(B2:B81,60)) is out: COUNT counts numeric cells; it does not test a condition.
Option C (=SUMIF(B2:B81,">60")) is out: SUMIF adds the qualifying values, not the number of them.
Option D (=COUNTA(B2:B81>60)) is out: COUNTA counts non-empty cells and the argument is not a valid criterion.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing SUMIF, which has a similar syntax but gives a sum.
So the answer is option A: =COUNTIF(B2:B81,">60").
questions.trap: Choosing SUMIF, which has a similar syntax but gives a sum.
wrongReasons: COUNT counts numeric cells; it does not test a condition
SUMIF adds the qualifying values, not the number of them
COUNTA counts non-empty cells and the argument is not a valid criterion

questions.text: In an Excel sheet, column A holds city names and column B holds sales. Which function counts the rows in which the city is "Delhi" AND the sales are above 50?
questions.explanation: COUNTIFS accepts several range–criteria pairs and counts the rows that satisfy all of them.
steps: Spot what the question tests: COUNTIFS vs COUNTIF.
Option A (COUNTIF) is out: It accepts only one range and one condition.
Option B (SUMIF) is out: It adds values instead of counting rows.
Option C (AVERAGEIF) is out: It returns an average, not a count.
Common slip to avoid: Using COUNTIF with a single criterion.
So the answer is option D: COUNTIFS.
questions.trap: Using COUNTIF with a single criterion.
wrongReasons: It accepts only one range and one condition
It adds values instead of counting rows
It returns an average, not a count

questions.text: Which Excel feature displays only the rows that meet a stated condition and hides the others, without deleting them?
questions.explanation: AutoFilter hides the rows that do not meet the condition; they return when the filter is cleared.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Sort vs Filter.
Option A (Sort) is out: It rearranges rows but hides none.
Option B (Data Validation) is out: It restricts what can be typed in a cell.
Option D (Freeze Panes) is out: It keeps rows or columns visible while scrolling.
Common slip to avoid: Confusing Sort with Filter.
So the answer is option C: Filter.
questions.trap: Confusing Sort with Filter.
wrongReasons: It rearranges rows but hides none
It restricts what can be typed in a cell
It keeps rows or columns visible while scrolling

questions.text: A user has applied Heading 1 and Heading 2 styles through a long Word report and wants an automatically updated list of headings with page numbers at the start. Which feature should be used?
questions.explanation: The Table of Contents feature reads the heading styles and builds the list, which can be refreshed with Update Field.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Table of Contents vs Index.
Option A (Index) is out: It lists selected terms with page numbers, not headings.
Option C (Cross-reference) is out: It links to one item in the document.
Option D (Bookmark) is out: It marks a location for later navigation.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing Index because it also shows page numbers.
So the answer is option B: Table of Contents.
questions.trap: Choosing Index because it also shows page numbers.
wrongReasons: It lists selected terms with page numbers, not headings
It links to one item in the document
It marks a location for later navigation

questions.text: In MS Word, which Review-tab feature records every edit made by a reviewer so that the author can later accept or reject each change?
questions.explanation: Track Changes marks insertions, deletions and formatting changes and allows each to be accepted or rejected.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Track Changes, Comments, Compare.
Option A (Comments) is out: They add notes but do not record edits.
Option B (Compare) is out: It builds a new document showing the differences between two files.
Option C (Restrict Editing) is out: It limits what others can change.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing Compare, which works on two saved versions.
So the answer is option D: Track Changes.
questions.trap: Choosing Compare, which works on two saved versions.
wrongReasons: They add notes but do not record edits
It builds a new document showing the differences between two files
It limits what others can change

questions.text: A presenter wants a company logo to appear in the same position on every slide of a deck, by editing it only once. Which view should be used?
questions.explanation: Slide Master view controls the layout shared by all slides; an object placed on the master appears on every slide.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Slide Master, layouts and themes.
Option B (Slide Sorter view) is out: It is for rearranging slides.
Option C (Notes Page view) is out: It is for speaker notes.
Option D (Reading view) is out: It is for viewing the deck on screen.
Common slip to avoid: Adding the logo slide by slide.
So the answer is option A: Slide Master view.
questions.trap: Adding the logo slide by slide.
wrongReasons: It is for rearranging slides
It is for speaker notes
It is for viewing the deck on screen

questions.text: In Windows File Explorer, which key combination opens the Properties dialog of the selected file?
questions.explanation: Alt + Enter opens the Properties dialog for the selected item.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Windows shortcuts: Alt+Enter, F2.
Option A (Ctrl + Enter) is out: It opens a selected item in some programs or adds line breaks.
Option B (Shift + Enter) is out: It is used for line breaks and alternative open commands.
Option D (F2) is out: It renames the selected file.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing F2, which also acts on the selected file.
So the answer is option C: Alt + Enter.
questions.trap: Choosing F2, which also acts on the selected file.
wrongReasons: It opens a selected item in some programs or adds line breaks
It is used for line breaks and alternative open commands
It renames the selected file

questions.text: In asymmetric encryption, a message is encrypted with the receiver's public key. Which key is needed to decrypt it?
questions.explanation: A message encrypted with a public key can be decrypted only with the matching private key, which the receiver keeps secret.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Public and private keys.
Option B (The sender's private key) is out: The sender's keys are used to sign, not to decrypt this message.
Option C (The sender's public key) is out: It is available to everyone and cannot decrypt.
Option D (The receiver's public key) is out: The same key cannot be used for both operations.
Common slip to avoid: Thinking the sender's key is needed.
So the answer is option A: The receiver's private key.
questions.trap: Thinking the sender's key is needed.
wrongReasons: The sender's keys are used to sign, not to decrypt this message
It is available to everyone and cannot decrypt
The same key cannot be used for both operations

questions.text: A digital signature on an electronic document primarily provides:
options: authentication of the sender and non-repudiation
questions.explanation: A signature created with the sender's private key proves who signed it and that the sender cannot later deny it.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Digital signature vs encryption.
Option B (confidentiality of the message content) is out: Encryption provides this; a signature does not hide the text.
Option C (compression of the document) is out: A signature does not compress data.
Option D (protection against power failure) is out: Not a function of signatures.
Common slip to avoid: Equating signing with encrypting.
So the answer is option A: authentication of the sender and non-repudiation.
questions.trap: Equating signing with encrypting.
wrongReasons: Encryption provides this; a signature does not hide the text
A signature does not compress data
Not a function of signatures

questions.text: Malware that disguises itself as useful software and opens a back door for an attacker, but does not copy itself to other files, is called a:
questions.explanation: A Trojan relies on being installed by the user in disguise and does not self-replicate.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Virus, worm, Trojan.
Option A (Worm) is out: A worm replicates by itself across networks.
Option C (File infector virus) is out: A virus attaches itself to other files.
Option D (Adware) is out: It shows advertisements, not a back door.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing worm because both can open back doors.
So the answer is option B: Trojan horse.
questions.trap: Choosing worm because both can open back doors.
wrongReasons: A worm replicates by itself across networks
A virus attaches itself to other files
It shows advertisements, not a back door

questions.text: Which of the following standards is used to encrypt and digitally sign email messages end to end?
questions.explanation: S/MIME uses certificates to encrypt and sign the content of a message; IMAP, POP3 and SMTP only move mail.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Email protocols vs security standards.
Option A (IMAP) is out: It retrieves mail from a server.
Option C (POP3) is out: It downloads mail from a server.
Option D (SMTP) is out: It sends mail between servers and does not encrypt the message by itself.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing a transfer protocol.
So the answer is option B: S/MIME.
questions.trap: Choosing a transfer protocol.
wrongReasons: It retrieves mail from a server
It downloads mail from a server
It sends mail between servers and does not encrypt the message by itself

questions.text: Which register holds the instruction that is currently being decoded and executed by the CPU?
questions.explanation: The Instruction Register stores the fetched instruction while the control unit decodes it.
steps: Spot what the question tests: CPU registers.
Option A (Program Counter) is out: It holds the address of the next instruction.
Option B (Memory Address Register) is out: It holds the address of the memory location to be accessed.
Option D (Memory Data Register) is out: It holds the data moved to or from memory.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing the Program Counter.
So the answer is option C: Instruction Register.
questions.trap: Choosing the Program Counter.
wrongReasons: It holds the address of the next instruction
It holds the address of the memory location to be accessed
It holds the data moved to or from memory

questions.text: A memory chip is organised as 16K × 16. How many address lines and data lines does it need?
questions.explanation: 16K = 2¹⁴ locations, so 14 address lines are needed; each word is 16 bits wide, so there are 16 data lines.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Memory capacity: 2ⁿ × word size.
Option A (16 address lines and 14 data lines) is out: The two numbers are swapped.
Option B (16 address lines and 16 data lines) is out: 16K needs 14 address lines, not 16.
Option C (14 address lines and 14 data lines) is out: The word size is 16 bits.
Common slip to avoid: Using the word size as the number of address lines.
So the answer is option D: 14 address lines and 16 data lines.
questions.trap: Using the word size as the number of address lines.
wrongReasons: The two numbers are swapped
16K needs 14 address lines, not 16
The word size is 16 bits

questions.text: Which bus carries the address of a memory location from the CPU to memory and moves in one direction only?
questions.explanation: The CPU sends addresses to memory over the address bus, which is unidirectional.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Address, data and control buses.
Option A (Data bus) is out: It is bidirectional.
Option C (Control bus) is out: It carries signals such as read and write.
Option D (Expansion bus) is out: It connects add-on cards.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing the data bus.
So the answer is option B: Address bus.
questions.trap: Choosing the data bus.
wrongReasons: It is bidirectional
It carries signals such as read and write
It connects add-on cards

questions.text: At which layer of the OSI model do routers work and logical (IP) addressing is handled?
questions.explanation: Routers forward packets between networks using IP addresses, which belong to the network layer.
steps: Spot what the question tests: OSI layers and devices.
Option A (Data link layer) is out: It handles physical (MAC) addressing.
Option B (Transport layer) is out: It handles end-to-end delivery and ports.
Option D (Session layer) is out: It manages dialogues between applications.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing the data link layer, where switches work.
So the answer is option C: Network layer.
questions.trap: Choosing the data link layer, where switches work.
wrongReasons: It handles physical (MAC) addressing
It handles end-to-end delivery and ports
It manages dialogues between applications

questions.text:
Consider the following statements.
I. DHCP assigns IP addresses to devices automatically.
II. DNS translates domain names into IP addresses.
III. ARP maps an IP address to a MAC address.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: All three describe the standard roles of DHCP, DNS and ARP.
steps: Spot what the question tests: DHCP, DNS, ARP.
Option A (I and II only) is out: III is also correct.
Option B (II and III only) is out: I is also correct.
Option C (I and III only) is out: II is also correct.
Common slip to avoid: Doubting ARP, which works inside a local network.
So the answer is option D: I, II and III.
questions.trap: Doubting ARP, which works inside a local network.
wrongReasons: III is also correct
I is also correct
II is also correct

questions.text: Which technology allows an application such as Excel to embed or link an object created in another application, such as a Word table?
questions.explanation: OLE lets one application hold or link to objects made by another, for example a chart or table.
steps: Spot what the question tests: OLE, ODBC, RPC.
Option B (ODBC) is out: It connects applications to databases.
Option C (RPC) is out: It lets a program call a procedure on another machine.
Option D (DNS) is out: It resolves names into addresses.
Common slip to avoid: Confusing it with database connectivity.
So the answer is option A: OLE (Object Linking and Embedding).
questions.trap: Confusing it with database connectivity.
wrongReasons: It connects applications to databases
It lets a program call a procedure on another machine
It resolves names into addresses

questions.text: A web-based email service that users access through a browser without installing or managing anything is an example of:
questions.explanation: SaaS delivers a ready-to-use application over the internet.
steps: Spot what the question tests: SaaS, PaaS, IaaS.
Option A (Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)) is out: IaaS supplies virtual machines and storage.
Option C (Platform as a Service (PaaS)) is out: PaaS supplies a platform for developers.
Option D (Desktop virtualisation) is out: This gives a remote desktop, not an application.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing IaaS or PaaS because all three are cloud models.
So the answer is option B: Software as a Service (SaaS).
questions.trap: Choosing IaaS or PaaS because all three are cloud models.
wrongReasons: IaaS supplies virtual machines and storage
PaaS supplies a platform for developers
This gives a remote desktop, not an application

questions.text: Which technique creates a point-in-time snapshot by preserving the original data blocks only when they are about to be changed?
questions.explanation: Copy-on-write saves the old block before it is overwritten, so a snapshot needs very little extra space.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Snapshots and copy-on-write.
Option A (Disk mirroring) is out: It keeps a full duplicate copy at all times.
Option B (Disk striping) is out: It spreads data across disks for speed.
Option D (Defragmentation) is out: It rearranges files to make them contiguous.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing mirroring because it also gives a second copy.
So the answer is option C: Copy-on-write.
questions.trap: Choosing mirroring because it also gives a second copy.
wrongReasons: It keeps a full duplicate copy at all times
It spreads data across disks for speed
It rearranges files to make them contiguous

questions.text: Which normal form removes the partial dependency of non-key attributes on part of a composite primary key?
questions.explanation: A relation is in 2NF when it is in 1NF and every non-key attribute depends on the whole of the primary key.
steps: Spot what the question tests: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF.
Option A (First Normal Form (1NF)) is out: It removes repeating groups and multivalued attributes.
Option B (Third Normal Form (3NF)) is out: It removes transitive dependencies.
Option C (Boyce–Codd Normal Form (BCNF)) is out: It requires every determinant to be a candidate key.
Common slip to avoid: Mixing up partial and transitive dependency.
So the answer is option D: Second Normal Form (2NF).
questions.trap: Mixing up partial and transitive dependency.
wrongReasons: It removes repeating groups and multivalued attributes
It removes transitive dependencies
It requires every determinant to be a candidate key
